newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean commercial banks cut prime lending rates.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean commercial banks cut prime lending rates.

text.p: South Korean commercial banks cut their prime rates by 0.25 percentage points on Friday as the government stepped up a drive to boost industrial competitiveness, bank officials said.
"We lowered our prime rates to 8.5 percent from 8.75 percent in compliance with government measures to reduce the cost of funds," said Park Young-suk, a spokesman at Cho Hung Bank.

The central bank, the Bank of Korea, prompted the prime rate cut in October by announcing cuts in bank reserve requirements by 1.9 percentage points to an average of 5.5 percent effective from Friday.

The government has said the current economic downturn stems from structural weakness -- low efficiency and high costs -- and boosting efficiency through cost-cutting and privatisation has become a matter of urgency.
South Korea's economy, hit by slowing exports, is expected to rise by about seven percent this year, down from nine percent growth last year, government officials said.

Banking analysts said the 0.25 percentage point cut in the prime rates would probably be the maximum commercial banks could afford without eroding profitability following the reserve ratio adjustment.
The reserve requirement is the portion of total deposits banks should set aside with the central bank.

"Other rates, including deposit rates, will also be lowered. The government has a mandate to bring down interest rates ahead of wider market opening," said Choo Joon-suk, an economist at Daewoo Research Institute.
Analysts said South Korea must lower interest rates before allowing freer capital movements when it joins the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).

Yields for three-year corporate bonds, South Korea's benchmark rates, hover around 12.10 percent, compared with 6.8 percent for the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond and 2.7 percent for Japan's 10-year state bond.
"We cannot open the capital market if high rates are not properly lowered," said Choo.
Cho Hung Bank, Korea First Bank, Hanil Bank and six other commercial banks cut their prime lending rates to 8.5 percent from 8.75 percent.
SEOULBANK, Hana Bank and five other commercial banks lowered or would soon lower their prime rates to 8.75 percent from 9.0 percent, bank officials said.
Two smaller banks cut their prime rates by 0.25 percentage points to 9.0 percent.
Economists said higher rates would attract capital inflows, which would in turn lead to appreciation of the local currency.
"A higher domestic currency will impede exports," said Choo.

Government planners, to help corporates facing profit falls because of falling prices of South Korea's main export items such as semiconductors, have drawn up a blueprint to lower costs for raising funds and manufacturing.
The nation's trade deficit is snowballing and could exceed $20 billion this year, compared with $10 billion in 1995.
In October, the finance ministry said it would cut domestic steel prices, freeze wage levels for senior government officials and open power generation to private-sector competition.
It also said the government would make it easier for big companies to borrow money overseas.
